title: Shipping industry urges governments to agree on global GHG regulations to provide regulatory certainty and incentivize maritime decarbonization
summary: Major shipping lobby groups are predictably calling for global IMO regulations, framing it as a push for "decarbonization." This demand for "regulatory certainty" primarily serves to prevent regional measures like FuelEU Maritime from imposing immediate, higher costs and stricter carbon intensity limits. Their insistence on "achievable" and "stable" frameworks is a transparent attempt to control the pace of change, delaying tangible HFO reductions and avoiding genuine accountability for ships failing their CII ratings.
content:
In advance of the UN International Maritime Organization (IMO) Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85), which meets in London from 30 November to 4 December 2026, this statement is made jointly by BIMCO, CLIA, IBIA, ICS, INTERCARGO, INTERFERRY, INTERTANKO, IPTA and WSC representing the global commercial shipping fleet.

The global shipping industry welcomes continuing efforts by all IMO Member States to agree on a global framework of practical, effective and fit for purpose regulations to help decarbonize international shipping and, whilst further improving energy efficiency, continue striving towards the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy goal of net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by or close to 2050.

The industry recognizes that all proposals put forward by governments, and the elements these contain, remain under consideration, but emphasizes the importance of an achievable, enforceable, and stable regulatory framework which reflects cost and availability and provides clear incentives for the development and deployment of commercially viable alternative fuels. The regulatory framework must also meaningfully support a safe energy transition through solutions which are data-driven and fuel and technology neutral.

Shipping is a global industry requiring global rules applied equally to all ships, regardless of flag, ownership, trade or business model. A coordinated global approach at IMO must lead to the avoidance of regulatory fragmentation or regional or national measures which result in duplication of compliance requirements for ships or multiple charges for the same GHG emissions. During the transition to lower-GHG fuels, only global regulation can ensure a level playing field.

The GHG reduction regulations to be adopted by IMO Member States must reward verifiable emission reductions and incentivize, financially and/or technically, further investments that advance maritime decarbonization. In addition, the regulations should also provide optional/flexible compliance mechanisms so that shipping companies, large and small, can manage the transition, recognizing the current unavailability of commercially viable zero/near-zero GHG fuels and technologies (ZNZs) for the majority of the existing fleet.

The shipping industry has invested billions of dollars in new ships capable of using alternative low GHG fuels, innovative technologies, and fuel-flexible solutions. The regulatory framework must support credible transition pathways for existing ships and technologies. Continued industry investment and effective implementation will depend on global regulatory certainty and the reliable production and cost-competitiveness of alternative fuels at scale.

Shipowners and other maritime stakeholders, including marine fuel producers, charterers, ports and financiers, all need investment certainty to support the maritime energy transition. An effective global regulatory framework agreed at the IMO is essential to provide clear predictable production pathways for further emissions reductions. To drive decarbonization across the shipping industry, support fleet renewal and financing decisions and maintain a global level playing field, the framework must be pragmatic, fit for purpose and underpinned by clear and enforceable obligations. This framework needs to be agreed as soon as practicable by the industry’s global regulator, the IMO.

Achieving an agreement at IMO will require constructive engagement by all Member States, on all sides of the debate, with the full range of alternative proposals on the table, to identify areas of convergence and to draw on their most effective elements, so as to develop a global solution that takes into account strategic ambition as well as market and technological readiness.
